milestone: Vela accelerator build-order item 3 — multi-agent namespace design (docs/vela/accelerator/constitutional-financial-services/09_CLAUDE_IMPLEMENTATION_HANDOFF_v0.2.md Phase 5)
problem: The handoff's Phase 5 requires that existing structures can bind a contributor/party handle, communication identity, permitted private-state namespace, execution context, disclosure recipients, and authority/mandate ref for a request going into a SHARED Vela application used by multiple agents/parties simultaneously — while explicitly warning against building a generalized IAM system. The Phase 0 inventory (`codexes/packs/agentiq/updates/2026-09-11_vela-accelerator-phase0-code-inventory.md` §2.3) had already found no per-party namespace primitive anywhere in `services/vela/`, `services/constitutionalCommerce/`, or `services/factor/factorConfidentialWorkload.ts`, and flagged (without resolving) whether the WASM guest itself subdivides its private state per contributor. Mid-task, the operator added a mandatory, verbatim acceptance test that governs this item: "Party A must be unable to cause Party B's confidential state to be read, combined, disclosed, or emitted unless the exact transaction/disclosure scope authorizes it" — this resolution's scope was expanded accordingly to (a) build and test a concrete gate enforcing that property wherever it CAN be enforced today, and (b) state precisely, as a load-bearing blocker rather than a buried caveat, the one part of the property this item cannot yet guarantee.
observedFailure: Not an observed runtime defect — this is a design-first investigation per the task's own framing: confirm whether a real isolation gap exists before treating Phase 5 as blocking, and if so, characterize its exact shape.

Re-reading `services/vela/wasm/projector/app/app.go` directly (rather than inferring from the TypeScript wrapper, per this task's explicit instruction) confirmed the crux fact precisely: `ApplicationInternalState{AppID, ProjectionsHandled}` (app.go:52-55) is ONE global blob per `applicationId`, with no per-party subdivision whatsoever. `ProcessRequest` (app.go:108-153) receives a real, protocol-given `sender *types.Address` (the on-chain caller identity — confirmed via `velaClientAdapter.ts`'s `RequestSubmitted(...,address indexed sender,...)` event) but uses it ONLY to address the encrypted `PlainEvent` back to the caller (app.go:149) — never to key, read, or write any persisted state. Today this is SAFE (not a leak) only because `project()` is a pure, stateless-per-call comparison with no persisted per-user field — but a future stateful multi-party guest (the Use Case Zero liquidity/coverage pilot) would have no existing mechanism to partition its state by contributor at all.

Confirmed `PreparedConfidentialProjection.identities` (the five-role `ConfidentialProjectionIdentitySet`) is carried on the TypeScript-side record but is NEVER serialized into the plaintext sent to the guest — `velaProjectionProvider.ts`'s `prepareProjection()` builds the plaintext from `request.confidentialInputs` + `request.publicContext` only (lines 128-138), and `VelaTransport.submitProcessRequest`/`submitAssetBearingProcessRequest` (velaTypes.ts) take only `applicationId` + ciphertext (+ asset) — no party/contributor identifier parameter at all.
rootCauses: The existing projector was built (correctly, for its own scope) as a single-participant, stateless-per-call comparison — it never needed a namespace because it never persists anything per-user. Multi-party isolation was never a live requirement until the accelerator's Use Case Zero pilot introduced the possibility of a stateful, multi-contributor guest sharing one `applicationId`.

No prior work had composed the repo's OWN identity primitives (`ConfidentialProjectionIdentitySet`) into a namespace-scoping key, because nothing yet needed to key anything by party — the identity set was built to separate CONSTITUTIONAL ROLES (who authorizes vs who decrypts vs who executes), not to solve state-partitioning, and no one had yet asked the state-partitioning question of it.
resolution: Confirmed the crux fact by reading `services/vela/wasm/projector/app/app.go` directly (not inferred from TypeScript): the guest has ONE global state blob per applicationId, no per-party keying, and the real on-chain `sender` address it already receives (a protocol-given, per-request contributor identity) is currently used only to address the encrypted verdict event — never to scope state.

Confirmed the five-role `ConfidentialProjectionIdentitySet` (types/confidentialProjection.ts) is the right SHAPE the handoff's Phase 5 fields map onto (contributor/party handle -> authorityPrincipal/confidentialPrivacyIdentity; communication identity -> confidentialRequester/executionSigner, already solved by build-order item 1's P-521 derivation; authority/mandate ref -> ConstitutionalAuthority.principalRef/mandateRef, already opaque/T0-safe in types/constitutionalCommerce.ts; disclosure recipients -> services/qubetalk/disclosurePolicy.ts's evaluateDisclosure(), an existing audience-subset selective-disclosure primitive reusable as a PATTERN) — no new IAM system is needed, confirming the handoff's own instruction.

Found and reused, rather than reinvented, the repo's EXISTING canonical namespaced-commitment helper `constitutionalRef(namespace, id)` (services/identity/personaReferences.ts) — the same sha256/16-hex derivation as `personaPublicRef()`, already used for passport/delegation/agent-standing refs (services/financialServices/constitutionalAuthorityAdapter.ts) — instead of writing a second hashing scheme, per CLAUDE.md's inv.engineering.036/037.

Added `services/vela/velaPartyNamespace.ts`: `deriveVelaPartyNamespaceRef(applicationId, {authorityPrincipal, confidentialPrivacyIdentity})` composes those two identity roles + the applicationId into one `constitutionalRef('vela-party-namespace', ...)` commitment — deterministic, one-way, fails closed on any missing input. This is additive: it is NOT wired into any live request path yet (no caller currently supplies a partyNamespaceRef to the guest), and it does NOT touch `types/confidentialProjection.ts` or `app.go`.

Added, in the SAME module, `VelaDisclosureScope` + `isVelaCrossPartyAccessAuthorized()` / `assertVelaCrossPartyAccessAuthorized()` — a fail-closed, per-`actionRef` (never a standing grant) gate implementing the operator's mandated property for TS-side evidence handling: self-access is always authorized; any other requester is authorized ONLY when explicitly named in `authorizedPartyNamespaceRefs` for that exact action; an absent or empty list denies every non-owner. Reuses the SAME isSubset/audience-membership SHAPE `services/qubetalk/disclosurePolicy.ts`'s `evaluateDisclosure()` already established for QubeTalk's own selective-disclosure boundary (generalised to opaque Vela namespace refs, not a literal import — QubeTalk's `sensitivity` vocabulary does not apply to Vela evidence).

Added `tests/vela-party-namespace.test.ts` (15 tests): the original 9 (determinism, within-app isolation, cross-app non-correlation, fail-closed on missing inputs, reuse of `constitutionalRef`, no plaintext leakage, no collisions across 500 samples) PLUS 6 new tests directly proving the operator's mandated acceptance property both ways — self-access always allowed; Party B denied reading/combining/disclosing Party A's state with no scope (the default); denied even with an explicit-but-empty authorized list; ALLOWED when the exact transaction scope explicitly names Party B (the legitimate multi-party-consent path — proving this is a real scope check, not a blanket lockout); an authorization for one actionRef does not carry over to a different actionRef; a third party never inherits an authorization scoped to a different requester.

Deliberately did NOT modify `services/vela/wasm/projector/app/app.go` or `types/confidentialProjection.ts` — see rejectedApproaches, and see this resolution's `unresolvedRisks` (elevated to a named HARD BLOCKER, not a buried caveat, per the operator's explicit instruction) for exactly what this leaves unresolved and why.
rejectedApproaches: Writing a new sha256 wrapper specific to Vela party-namespace refs — rejected: `constitutionalRef()` already exists, is already the canonical namespaced-commitment helper for exactly this shape of problem (a non-persona identifier needing a T2-safe, one-way, namespaced ref), and a second hashing scheme would be the exact 'parallel implementation of an existing capability' inv.engineering.036/037 forbids.

Adding a `partyNamespaceRef` field to `ConfidentialProjectionIdentitySet` or `ConfidentialProjectionRequest`/`PreparedConfidentialProjection` (types/confidentialProjection.ts) — rejected for THIS item: that module is documented as encoding four standing rulings the operator ruled on 2026-08-22, and locking a specific field shape into that frozen domain seam before the Use Case Zero pilot's actual multi-party state model is designed (Phase 11, the NEXT build-order item) risks baking in a shape that has to be redesigned once that model exists. The derivation function is deliberately kept freestanding so Phase 11 can decide HOW to thread it (a new field, a publicContext key, or something the new/extended guest design suggests) without this item pre-deciding that for it.

Modifying `services/vela/wasm/projector/app/app.go` to key `ApplicationInternalState` by contributor now — rejected: today's projector is deliberately stateless-per-call (its own header: 'it moves no funds and holds no balances of its own'); there is no existing multi-party stateful guest to retrofit, and building one (or deciding whether the existing guest is extended vs. a new one is shipped) is explicitly Phase 11's job (the Use Case Zero vertical slice, this repo's next build-order item), not this design item's. Per this task's own instruction, a guest-side change bigger than this item should absorb is reported as a scoped follow-up rather than attempted as a speculative WASM rewrite with no real caller yet.

Wiring `evaluateDisclosure()` (services/qubetalk/disclosurePolicy.ts) directly into the Vela request path as the 'disclosure recipients' mechanism — rejected as premature: QubeTalk's disclosure primitive operates over `DisclosureContextItem[]` + participant ids for its own Communications Membrane domain; reusing its PATTERN (audience-subset evaluation) for Vela evidence/receipt disclosure is sound, but wiring the literal function in now, before Phase 11 defines what a Vela evidence disclosure recipient list actually needs to contain, would be speculative coupling between two domains that happen to share a shape, not yet a requirement either domain has.
unresolvedRisks: HARD BLOCKER FOR PHASE 11 (Use Case Zero vertical slice) — NOT a buried caveat: the TS-side disclosure gate added here enforces the operator's mandated property ONLY for evidence handling that happens AFTER a request leaves the Vela guest. Today's guest (`app.go`) receives NO disclosure scope in its payload at all (`prepareProjection()` never serialises `identities`) and is stateless/single-participant, so there is nothing to protect yet — but the INSTANT Phase 11 builds a stateful guest that combines or reads more than one contributor's private input, if that guest does not itself check an authorized-scope list BEFORE combining data INSIDE THE ENCLAVE, the required property is violated at the point of computation, and no TS-side wrapper outside the TEE can retroactively fix that once evidence has left it. This MUST be resolved — via (a) a guest-side change so the guest receives and enforces an authorized-namespace-refs list before combining any two parties' inputs, or (b) an operator ruling that the first vertical slice never asks one guest call to combine two parties' confidential inputs at all (each party's state stays in its own guest call; any cross-party combination happens only in an already-consented frozen envelope BEFORE submission) — BEFORE any underwriting/multi-party vertical slice work proceeds. See the companion update doc for this stated as an explicit operator/Vela-team decision with both options named.

The exact architecture decision Phase 11 needs before `deriveVelaPartyNamespaceRef`'s output is ever actually consumed by a guest — does the Use Case Zero multi-party pilot extend the existing stateless `app.go` projector, or ship as a separate guest? — remains genuinely open (Phase 0's own open question #2, unresolved by this item on purpose) and is restated precisely, with options, in the companion update doc for operator/Vela-team decision. This is the SAME decision that would close the hard blocker above, from the guest-architecture side.

The disclosure gate's correctness (self-access always allowed; every other requester denied absent an explicit, action-scoped authorization) is proven for the gate itself (15 tests, including 6 for the mandated property) but nothing yet CALLS this gate from a real evidence-combination code path, because no such path exists yet (Phase 11 has not been built) — this is intentional (nothing to wire it into safely without a design that would be redesigned once Phase 11 exists), but it means the gate is proven correct in isolation, not proven to be actually invoked everywhere it will eventually need to be.

This gap is already, independently, a live Vela-team-facing question, not only an internal one: `docs/vela/accelerator/constitutional-financial-services/08_VELA_OFFICE_HOURS_QUESTIONS_2026-09-11.md` Priority A questions 3-4 ask the Vela team directly what state-namespace pattern it recommends for a multi-agent app, and whether one request can safely include contributions from several users/agents 'if the WASM enforces the logical authorization and disclosure rules' — as of this investigation, no Vela-team answer is recorded there. The hard blocker above is gated on BOTH an internal operator ruling AND (if guest-side enforcement is chosen) Vela's own answer to this exact question.
